moed_katan-4a-21-21.note: Ravina and Rabba Tosefa'a were walking along the road and saw a man drawing water with a bucket during the intermediate days of a Festival. Rabba Tosefa'a told Ravina to excommunicate him. Ravina objected that a teaching allows one to draw for vegetables in order to eat them. Rabba Tosefa'a answered that the word there does not mean drawing water at all. In the discussion that follows he explains it as thinning out vegetables, and when Ravina cites a teaching that explicitly allows drawing water, he takes back his view.
moed_katan-4a-21-21.why: A teaching just quoted allows watering vegetables during the intermediate days in order to eat them, but not to improve their looks. The story turns on what the key word in that teaching means.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who defended the man drawing water.

people.name: Rabba Tosefa'a
people.about: A Sage who wanted the man excommunicated.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is allowed and some is not.
To place a person under a ban, cutting him off from the community for a time.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

moed_katan-8a-18-18.note: Rav Kahana reported, through Rav Yehuda, an incident Rav told: a man saved up money to go up to Jerusalem for a pilgrimage Festival. A professional eulogizer came and stood at the door of his house, and the man's wife took the money and gave it to him. The man then held back and did not go. At that time the Sages ruled that one may not stir up mourning for a dead relative, or eulogize him, in the thirty days before a pilgrimage Festival.
moed_katan-8a-18-18.why: The mishna forbids lamenting the dead in the thirty days before a Festival, and the Gemara asks why thirty. Rav's story gives one reason, money for the Festival being spent; Shmuel then offers another, that grief lasts thirty days.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose account this is, passed on by Rav Yehuda and Rav Kahana.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: He transmitted the account from Rav.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: He reported the account in Rav Yehuda's name.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot or Sukkot, when people went up to the Temple in Jerusalem.
A professional mourner paid to deliver laments for the dead.
Stirring up mourning again for a relative who has died.

moed_katan-9a-19-22.note: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts, studied the laws of oaths in Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's study hall. They took leave of him in the evening and came back to take leave again in the morning. He asked whether they had not already done so. They said he had taught them that a student who takes leave and then stays the night in the same town must take leave again, learned from two verses on when Solomon sent the people home. Rabbi Shimon told his son that these were men of distinction and he should go to them for a blessing. The son found them puzzling over two verses in Proverbs that seem to contradict each other. What happened when he came to them follows later.
moed_katan-9a-19-22.why: The Gemara has just been expounding the verses about Solomon dedicating the Temple and sending the people home; the two students draw a rule of conduct from those same verses.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: One of two students who took leave of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai twice.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: The other student.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Their teacher, who sent his son to them for a blessing.

people.name: Solomon
people.about: The king in the verses the students cite.

terms.meaning: A student's formal farewell to his teacher.
The translation's phrase for wise and learned men.

moed_katan-9b-3-4.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's son came to the two Sages, Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda son of converts, and told them his father had sent him for a blessing. They said: may you sow and not reap, bring in and not take out, take out and not bring in; may your house be destroyed and your lodging inhabited, your table be confused, and may you not see a new year. He went home and told his father they had not only failed to bless him but had hurt him. His father asked what they said, then told him these were all blessings: to sow and not reap means to have sons who do not die; to bring in and not take out means to bring brides for your sons and have the sons live; to take out and not bring in means to marry off daughters whose husbands live, so they do not return home.
moed_katan-9b-3-4.why: This finishes the episode in which Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai sent his son to the two Sages for a blessing. The Gemara then tells a second story of a blessing whose meaning was hidden.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: One of the two Sages who gave the son a blessing that sounded like a curse.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: The other Sage.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: The father, who explained that the words were blessings.

moed_katan-9b-7-8.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta took leave of Rav, and his father told him to go back for a blessing. Rav said: may it be God's will that you neither shame others nor feel ashamed. At home his father asked what Rav had said, and he answered that it was just words. His father told him Rav had given him the blessing God gave Israel, and God gave it twice, as Joel writes: My people shall never be ashamed, and again, My people shall never be ashamed.
moed_katan-9b-7-8.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's son, whose blessing sounded like a curse; the Gemara adds another blessing whose weight the one receiving it missed.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Ḥalafta
people.about: He was blessed by Rav and thought it was nothing special.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who gave the blessing.

people.name: God
people.about: His blessing of Israel in Joel is the one Rav repeated.

moed_katan-9b-20-20.note: Rav Beivai had a daughter and spread lime on her body, one limb at a time, to remove her hair; when he married her off he received four hundred dinars for her. A gentile neighbor who had a daughter spread lime on her all at once, and she died. The neighbor said: Beivai killed my daughter. Rav Naḥman said: Rav Beivai drinks beer, so his daughters need lime; we who do not drink beer, our daughters do not need it.
moed_katan-9b-20-20.why: The mishna lets women carry on their cosmetic treatments during the intermediate days of a Festival, and the Gemara has been describing how girls removed body hair with lime, flour or oil. This story about lime follows.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: A Sage who treated his daughter with lime, limb by limb.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who said beer drinkers' daughters need such treatment and others' do not.

terms.meaning: A caustic powder that was smeared on the skin to remove hair.
Coins; four hundred was a large sum given at her marriage.

moed_katan-11a-13-13.note: During the intermediate days of a Festival the Bedita River overflowed and left fish stranded on its banks. Everyone went out, caught fish and brought them home, and Rava permitted them to salt some of them.
moed_katan-11a-13-13.why: The mishna allows preserving food during the intermediate days only if it can be eaten on the Festival. Abaye challenges Rava's permission on just that ground, and Rava answers that fish which would spoil count as property about to be lost.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who allowed people to salt the fish they caught.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is allowed and some is not.
Food such as pickles or salted fish, prepared to keep for later.

moed_katan-11b-11-12.note: Maryon son of Ravin and Mar son of Rav Aḥa son of Rava owned a team of oxen together, one ox each. A death struck Mar's family, and he unhitched his ox from the team so no work would be done with it while he mourned. Rav Ashi said: does a great man like Mar behave this way? Even if he does not mind his own loss, does he not mind his partner's? A teaching says animals hired out to others may go on working. The Gemara explains that Mar held that an important person is different.
moed_katan-11b-11-12.why: A baraita has been setting out what work may be done for a mourner, including that animals hired or leased to others may keep working. Rav Ashi measures Mar's conduct against that rule.

people.name: Maryon, son of Ravin
people.about: Co-owner of the team of oxen.

people.name: Mar, son of Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: Co-owner who, while in mourning, took his ox out of the team.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who criticized Mar for causing his partner a loss.

terms.meaning: A polite way of saying a relative died and he was in mourning.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
A leading figure may hold himself to a stricter standard than the law requires, so others do not take it lightly.

moed_katan-12a-3-3.note: Gentile contractors built a mansion for Mar Zutra son of Rav Naḥman outside the Sabbath limit. Rav Safra and Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana happened to come there but would not go into it; the translation explains this was because it had been built on the Sabbath. Some say that Mar Zutra himself did not go into it either.
moed_katan-12a-3-3.why: Shmuel has just ruled that gentile contractors may work for a Jew on the Sabbath outside the Sabbath limit. The Gemara asks why these Sages avoided the house anyway and answers that an important person is different, or that Mar Zutra had supplied the straw for the bricks.

people.name: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage for whom the mansion was built.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage who would not enter the mansion.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana
people.about: A Sage who came with Rav Safra and also stayed out.

terms.meaning: Workers paid for a finished job rather than by the day, who set their own hours.
The distance outside a town, about two thousand cubits, within which one may walk on the Sabbath.

moed_katan-12b-14-14.note: Rav Ashi owned a forest in Shelaniya and went to cut it down during the intermediate days of the Festival. Rav Sheila of Shelaniya asked him whether he was relying on Rav's ruling that a person may chop down a palm tree then even if he needs only its sawdust, when Abaye had cursed such behavior. Rav Ashi answered that he had not heard that, a polite way of saying he did not agree. Then his ax slipped and nearly cut off his leg. He stopped, and came back to cut the forest only after the Festival.
moed_katan-12b-14-14.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav's permission to chop down a palm tree on the intermediate days, and Abaye's curse on it. This story shows what happened to a Sage who acted on the lenient ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who owned a forest and set out to cut it down during the Festival.

people.name: Rav Sheila from Shelaniya
people.about: A local Sage who questions Rav Ashi's tree cutting.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who cursed chopping down trees on the intermediate days for so small a need.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling, reported by Rav Hananel, allowed cutting down a palm tree for its sawdust.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, between the holy first and last days. Ordinary work is restricted on them, but some work is allowed to prevent a loss.

moed_katan-12b-16-16.note: Rabbi Yannai had an orchard whose fruit became ready to harvest during the intermediate days of the Festival, and he harvested it then. The next year everyone delayed harvesting their orchards until the intermediate days. That year Rabbi Yannai declared his orchard ownerless.
moed_katan-12b-16-16.why: The Gemara has been gathering cases of farm work on the intermediate days. Right after this, the Mishna rules that someone who plans his work for those days from the outset must lose what that work produces.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: A Sage whose harvest during the Festival led others to put off their own harvests until then.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, between the holy first and last days. Ordinary work is restricted on them, but some work is allowed to prevent a loss.
Gave up ownership of the produce, so that anyone could come and take it.

moed_katan-16a-12-13.note: A butcher behaved disrespectfully toward Rav Tuvi bar Mattana. Abaye and Rava were appointed to the case and ostracized him. Later the butcher went and made peace with Rav Tuvi. Abaye did not know what to do: the ban had not yet lasted the usual thirty days, but the Sages wanted to buy meat at his shop. He asked Rav Idi bar Avin, who quoted Shmuel: a shofar blast puts a ban in force and a shofar blast releases it. Abaye answered that this applies to someone who ignored a money judgment, but for disrespect the ban must stay in force for thirty days.
moed_katan-16a-12-13.why: The Gemara has just said that someone who ignores a money judgment is warned three times first, while someone who disrespects a scholar is ostracized at once. Abaye applies the same difference to lifting a ban, and the Gemara then infers his view on who may release one.

people.name: Rav Tuvi bar Mattana
people.about: The Sage the butcher treated with disrespect.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: One of the two Sages who ostracized the butcher; he weighs whether to release him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The other Sage appointed to the case.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: The Sage Abaye asks for a precedent; he quotes Shmuel.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
A ram's horn. Its blast was sounded when a ban was announced, and could be sounded again to release it.

moed_katan-16a-20-21.note: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and bar Kappara were studying together and hit a difficult point of law. Rabbi Shimon said it needed his father to explain it. Bar Kappara answered, somewhat mockingly: and what can Rabbi say about this? Rabbi Shimon told his father, who became angry. When bar Kappara later came to visit, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said to him: Bar Kappara, I do not know you at all. Bar Kappara understood he had given offense, and treated himself as admonished for thirty days.
moed_katan-16a-20-21.why: A baraita says admonition lasts seven days, and Rav Hisda said a Babylonian ban equals an admonition in the Land of Israel. The Gemara uses this story to challenge that admonition there lasts only seven days, since bar Kappara kept thirty.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he reports bar Kappara's remark to his father.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage who studies with Rabbi Shimon and makes a mocking remark about his father.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; father of Rabbi Shimon, offended by bar Kappara's words.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who compares the Babylonian ban to the admonition of the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.
A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.

moed_katan-16a-22-22.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decreed that students not be taught in the marketplace: just as a thigh is kept covered, Torah should be kept hidden. Rabbi Hiyya went out and taught his nephews Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana in the marketplace. Rabbi was angered and greeted him with: Iyya, who is calling you outside? Rabbi Hiyya took himself to be admonished for thirty days. On the thirtieth day Rabbi sent for him, then sent word not to come. Rabbi Hiyya came, saying he had seen the first messenger but not the second, and Rabbi applied to him the verse about God making even a man's enemies be at peace with him. Asked why he taught in public, Rabbi Hiyya cited Wisdom cries aloud in the streets; Rabbi told him he had not understood the verse.
moed_katan-16a-22-22.why: The Gemara is testing how long an admonition lasted in the Land of Israel; like bar Kappara before him, Rabbi Hiyya keeps thirty days. It explains Rabbi's two messages as a change of mind on whether part of a day counts as a whole day.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; he forbids teaching students in the marketplace and is angered when Rabbi Hiyya does so.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who teaches his two nephews in the marketplace against Rabbi's decree.

people.name: Rav
people.about: One of Rabbi Hiyya's two nephews, taught in the marketplace.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's other nephew, taught alongside Rav.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.

terms.term: part of the day is like an entire day
terms.meaning: A legal principle that once a day has begun, it can count as a full day, for example the last day of a waiting period.

moed_katan-16b-11-11.note: Mar Ukva, the Exilarch, used to accompany Shmuel to his lodgings every day, as a student honors his teacher. One day Mar Ukva was so absorbed in a court case that he did not notice Shmuel walking behind him, escorting him instead. When Mar Ukva reached his home, Shmuel said: Is it not enough for you? Release me, Master, from my obligation. Mar Ukva understood that Shmuel had taken offense, and treated himself as admonished for one day.
moed_katan-16b-11-11.why: The Gemara asked how long an admonition lasts in Babylonia and answered one day; Mar Ukva's single day of self-imposed admonition is its proof.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The Exilarch and chief judge, who honored Shmuel as his teacher.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage greater than Mar Ukva in Torah, who honored Mar Ukva for his office.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who also sat as its chief judge.
A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.

moed_katan-16b-12-12.note: A woman was sitting by a path with her leg stretched out, sifting barley. A Torah scholar passed by and she did not move out of his way. He said: How rude is that woman! She came to Rav Nahman. He asked whether she had heard the word excommunication from the scholar's mouth. She said no. He told her to go and observe an admonition for one day.
moed_katan-16b-12-12.why: The Gemara has said that an admonition in Babylonia lasts one day, proving it from Mar Ukva's case. Here a Sage gives that one-day length as a ruling.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage the woman asks whether the scholar's words had put her under a ban.

terms.meaning: A milder rebuke than a formal ban. The rebuked person keeps his distance and behaves humbly for a set time.
The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.

moed_katan-17a-3-10.note: A Torah scholar had a bad reputation. Rav Yehuda was torn: the Sages needed him, but leaving him alone would desecrate God's name. Rabba bar bar Hana quoted Rabbi Yohanan: seek Torah only from a teacher who is like an angel of the Lord. So Rav Yehuda ostracized him. On his deathbed Rav Yehuda laughed when the scholar visited, glad that he had not flattered even such a man. After Rav Yehuda died, Rabbi Ami was about to release the scholar, but Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani objected, and Rabbi Zeira took the elder's rare visit as a sign. The scholar left in tears. A wasp stung him on his penis and he died. The burial caves of the pious would not accept him; the caves of the judges did.
moed_katan-17a-3-10.why: The discussion is about who may impose a ban and how binding it is. This case upholds a ban on a needed scholar even after the Sage who imposed it had died, and the Gemara then explains why he still earned the judges' caves.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who ostracizes the scholar of bad reputation.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Quotes Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that settles Rav Yehuda's doubt.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Yehuda Nesia to examine the case; he does not release the ban.

people.name: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani
people.about: An elder who argues that Rav Yehuda's ban must be taken seriously.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sees the elder's rare appearance in the study hall as a sign not to release the ban.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
To bring God and the Torah into disrepute, for example when a known scholar behaves badly and nothing is done.

moed_katan-17a-12-12.note: A maidservant in the house of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw a man striking his adult son. She declared that the man be excommunicated, because he was breaking the command not to place a stumbling block before the blind. A baraita explains that this verse speaks of a man who strikes his adult son, since the son may be provoked to strike his father back. This telling does not say what came of her ban.
moed_katan-17a-12-12.why: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani had pointed to this maidservant's ban to argue against releasing the scholar Rav Yehuda had ostracized; the Gemara now tells the case he alluded to.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, in whose house the maidservant worked.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
A Torah command (Leviticus 19:14), read here as forbidding anyone to lead another person into sin.

moed_katan-17a-13-15.note: Reish Lakish was guarding an orchard when a man came and ate figs. Reish Lakish shouted at him, but the man paid no attention, so Reish Lakish declared him excommunicated. The man answered: on the contrary, let you be excommunicated; if I owe you money, do I owe you a ban? Reish Lakish went to the study hall, and the Sages told him the man's ban was valid and his own was not. To be released he should go to the man, but Reish Lakish did not know who he was. So they sent him to the Nasi, citing a baraita that someone banned by a person he does not know may be released by the Nasi.
moed_katan-17a-13-15.why: Like the maidservant's ban just before it, this is a ban declared on the spot without a court. Here the Sages rule a ban used over a money matter is void, and say how to be freed from a ban when the one who imposed it is unknown.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who was guarding an orchard for pay and banned a man who ate the figs.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.
The president of the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish court, and the leader of the Jews in the Land of Israel.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.

moed_katan-17a-23-23.note: Rav Yosef said that a ban cast even on a dog's tail will do its work. It was told that a dog kept eating the Sages' shoes. Not knowing who was doing it, they excommunicated the culprit. The dog's tail caught fire and burned.
moed_katan-17a-23-23.why: The Gemara has been describing how deeply a ban takes hold of a person: Shmuel likens it to fat soaked into an oven, Reish Lakish says it enters all 248 organs. This story shows its force reaching even an animal.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who says a ban works even on a dog's tail.

terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ban, cutting a person off from the community until it is lifted.

moed_katan-17a-24-25.note: A violent man was tormenting a Torah scholar, who came to Rav Yosef. Rav Yosef told him to ostracize the man, but the scholar said he was afraid of him. Rav Yosef told him to write out a ban against him; the scholar said he was even more afraid. So Rav Yosef told him to put the written ban in a jug, set it in a cemetery, and sound a thousand shofar blasts over forty days. The scholar did so. The jug burst and the violent man died.
moed_katan-17a-24-25.why: It follows Rav Yosef's teaching that a ban works even on a dog's tail. Here a ban pronounced in secret, where no one hears it, still takes effect, and the Gemara explains why the shofar is sounded with a ban.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the tormented scholar turns to, who tells him how to ban the man without being seen.

terms.meaning: A ban placed on someone by a court or a Sage: others keep away from him until it is lifted. Excommunication is the more severe form.
A ram's horn, sounded when a ban was announced. The Gemara links its name to the punishment a ban brings.

moed_katan-18a-1-2.note: A close relative of Pinehas, Shmuel's brother, died, and Shmuel came to console him. Seeing his long nails, Shmuel asked why he did not cut them. Pinehas answered: if it were your loss, would you take it so lightly? His words came true like an error from a ruler: soon a relative of Shmuel died. When Pinehas came to console him, Shmuel took his own cut nails, threw them in Pinehas's face, and said: Do you not know that a covenant is made with the lips?
moed_katan-18a-1-2.why: The Gemara is debating whether a mourner may cut his nails; Shmuel ruled leniently in mourning and is shown acting on it. Rabbi Yohanan's proof that spoken words shape events follows.

people.name: Pinehas
people.about: Shmuel's brother, who as a mourner let his nails grow.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who held that a mourner may cut his nails.

terms.term: a covenant is made with the lips
terms.meaning: A saying that what a person speaks aloud can bring it about, so one should be careful what one says.

terms.term: like an error from a ruler
terms.meaning: A phrase from Ecclesiastes 10:5, used here for words spoken carelessly that come true anyway.

moed_katan-18b-13-13.note: Rava heard a man praying: grant me so-and-so as a wife. Rava told him not to pray that way: if she is meant for you, you will not lose her, and if not, you will come to deny the Lord. Later, after the man married her, Rava heard him pray that either he die before her or she die before him. Rava said to him: Did I not tell you not to pray about this?
moed_katan-18b-13-13.why: Shmuel had said a man may betroth a woman during the Festival lest another man come first, though matches are decreed by a Divine Voice; the Gemara explains the fear as a rival praying to change the decree, and this is such a prayer.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who warns a man against praying for a particular woman.

terms.meaning: The Talmud's usual phrase for praying to God for something.

moed_katan-20a-15-15.note: Rabbi Tzadok's father died in Ginzak, and he was told only three years later. He asked Elisha ben Avuya and the elders with him what to do, and Elisha ben Avuya told him to observe the seven-day and thirty-day mourning. Likewise, when Rabbi Ahiyya's son died abroad, Rabbi Ahiyya sat in mourning for seven and thirty days.
moed_katan-20a-15-15.why: Rava ruled that late news of a death needs only one day of mourning; Rav Natan objected with a baraita requiring full mourning for a parent. Rava answers that this view belonged to a few individuals, citing these cases.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who cites these cases to show the strict view was held only by individuals.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Learned of his father's death three years late.

people.name: Elisha ben Avuya
people.about: The Sage who told Rabbi Tzadok to observe full mourning.

people.name: Rabbi Ahiyya
people.about: A Sage who sat seven and thirty days of mourning for his son who died abroad.

terms.meaning: The two stages of Jewish mourning: an intense first week, and a lighter period lasting to the thirtieth day.

moed_katan-20a-16-16.note: Rav was Rabbi Hiyya's nephew twice over, the son of his brother and of his sister. When Rav came to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Hiyya asked him: Is your father alive? Rav answered: Is my mother alive? Rabbi Hiyya asked: Is your mother alive? Rav answered: Is my father alive? Rabbi Hiyya understood that both had died. He told his servant to take off his shoes, and then to carry his clothes after him to the bathhouse.
moed_katan-20a-16-16.why: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Ahiyya mourned seven and thirty days for late news, since Rabbi Hiyya here mourned briefly. It learns that late news needs one day of mourning and that part of a day counts as a day, then says Hiyya and Ahiyya are two people.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's nephew, son of both his brother and his sister, who avoids saying outright that his parents died.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle, who works out from Rav's answers that his brother and sister have died.

terms.meaning: A mourner may not wear leather shoes, so removing them is a first act of mourning.

moed_katan-20b-11-11.note: Mar Ukva's brother-in-law, the son of his father-in-law, died, and Mar Ukva meant to observe the seven-day and thirty-day mourning for him. Rav Huna came to his house, found him mourning, and said: Do you want to eat mourners' food? The Sages said that a man mourns out of honor for his wife only for his father-in-law or mother-in-law.
moed_katan-20b-11-11.why: The Gemara is asking when one must join a relative's mourning. Rav Huna's limit is then backed by two baraitot, read as separating a wife's parents from her other relatives.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A Sage who began mourning for his wife's brother.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who tells Mar Ukva he need not mourn for his brother-in-law.

terms.meaning: The meals eaten by people in mourning. Rav Huna is asking, in effect, whether Mar Ukva wants to take on mourning he is not required to keep.

moed_katan-20b-15-15.note: Ameimar's grandson, his son's son, died, and Ameimar tore his garment over him. When his son came, Ameimar tore his garment again in his son's presence. Then he remembered that he had torn it while sitting, so he stood up and tore it again standing.
moed_katan-20b-15-15.why: The Gemara has been discussing mourning alongside a relative who is in mourning, as Ameimar does for his son. Rav Ashi then asks him for the source that tearing must be done standing.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage whose grandson died and who tore his garment three times.

terms.meaning: A Jewish mourning rite: on hearing of a close relative's death, the mourner tears his clothing.

moed_katan-21a-6-6.note: Rabbi Yosei's son died in the town of Tzippori. Rabbi Yosei went into the study hall and taught there for the entire day.
moed_katan-21a-6-6.why: A baraita lists what a mourner may not do, among them work, bathing and studying Torah, but adds that if the public needs him he need not hold back from teaching. Rabbi Yosei's day of teaching is its example.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who taught in the study hall on the day his son died.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
The house of study, where the Sages taught Torah to students and the public.

moed_katan-21a-8-8.note: When Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai's son died, he went into the study hall. Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya came in and sat beside him. Rabbi Yehuda whispered his lecture to Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, who whispered it to the disseminator, and the disseminator announced it to the public.
moed_katan-21a-8-8.why: Rav told the mourning Rabba bar bar Hana that a mourner who teaches may not have an interpreter beside him. The Gemara asks how he can be heard, and answers with this case.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai
people.about: A Sage who taught in the study hall after his son died.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya
people.about: A Sage who sat beside him and passed his words on.

terms.meaning: The speaker who repeated a Sage's lecture aloud to the crowd, since the Sage spoke quietly.

moed_katan-21b-4-5.note: When the sons of Rabbi Akiva died, all the Jews came to eulogize them with a great eulogy. As the crowd was about to leave, Rabbi Akiva stood on a large bench and addressed them as 'our brothers, the house of Israel.' He said that even had his two sons been bridegrooms, he would have been consoled by the honor shown them; the people had not come for Akiva the man, since there are many Akivas in the marketplace, but out of respect for the Torah. Their reward was doubled, he said, and he sent them home in peace.
moed_katan-21b-4-5.why: A teaching says a mourner may not greet anyone in the first three days. The Gemara challenges this with Rabbi Akiva, who greeted the crowd on the day of his loss, and answers that respect for the public is different.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage whose two sons died; he addresses the crowd that came to eulogize them.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one to test a ruling.
A public speech of mourning praising the dead, given at or around the funeral.

moed_katan-23a-6-6.note: When the wife of Yosef the Priest died, he said to her sister at the cemetery, right after the funeral: 'Go and care for your sister's children,' hinting that he wished to marry her at once. Even so, he did not have sexual relations with her until a long time later. Rav Pappa explains that 'a long time' means after thirty days.
moed_katan-23a-6-6.why: The Gemara has just taught that a widower must wait three Festivals before remarrying, unless he has young children who need care. Yosef the Priest's case shows that exception, and that he still held back from relations during the thirty-day mourning period.

people.name: Yosef the Priest
people.about: A man whose wife died; he asks her sister to care for the children, hinting he will marry her.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who explains that 'a long time' in the story means thirty days.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a member of the hereditary priestly family descended from Aaron.

moed_katan-24a-3-3.note: Rafram bar Pappa quotes a teaching from Evel Rabbati, a tractate devoted to the laws of mourning: a mourner may not have sexual relations during his days of mourning. It tells of a man who did so, and after his death pigs dragged away his corpse.
moed_katan-24a-3-3.why: The Sages had quoted Shmuel that a mourner who has relations is liable to death at the hand of Heaven, and Rav Pappa corrected them that it is only prohibited. This incident, quoted from a mourning tractate, shows how seriously the prohibition was taken.

people.name: Rafram bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage who reports the teaching and the incident from Evel Rabbati.

terms.meaning: A separate early tractate devoted to the laws of mourning and death, outside the main Talmud.
The first period after a close relative's burial, during which a mourner refrains from work, bathing, marital relations and other ordinary activities.

moed_katan-24a-9-9.note: When Shmuel was told that Rav had died, he tore twelve garments over him and said: 'The man I was in fear of has gone.' In the same way, when Rabbi Yohanan was told that Rabbi Hanina had died, he tore thirteen expensive wool garments and said the same words.
moed_katan-24a-9-9.why: Shmuel ruled that tearing clothes not done at the moment of most intense grief is not proper tearing. The Gemara challenges him with these Sages, who tore when the news reached them later, and answers that a Sage's death is different, since his teachings keep renewing the grief.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who tears twelve garments on hearing of Rav's death.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great Sage whose death is reported to Shmuel; Shmuel says he was in fear of him.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who tears thirteen wool garments on hearing of Rabbi Hanina's death.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose death is reported to Rabbi Yohanan.

terms.meaning: Tearing one's clothing as a sign of grief, a traditional Jewish mourning rite.

moed_katan-25a-6-7.note: When Rav Safra died, the other Sages did not tear their garments over him, saying they had not learned from him. Abaye told them the rule speaks of any Torah scholar, not only one's own teacher, and besides, Rav Safra's teachings were in their mouths every day in the study hall. They thought it was now too late, but Abaye said one must tear as long as the eulogy goes on. When they then wanted to tear at once, Abaye told them a scholar's honor is at his eulogy, so they should wait for it.
moed_katan-25a-6-7.why: The discussion is working out over whom one must tear one's clothes, including a Torah scholar or one present at the moment of death. The Rav Safra case shows how the rule for a scholar is applied, including when the tearing should happen.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Torah scholar who died; the Sages at first did not tear their clothes over him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who corrects the others about tearing their clothes for Rav Safra.

terms.meaning: The beit midrash, the house of study where Sages and students learned and debated Torah.
A public speech of mourning praising the dead.

moed_katan-25a-8-13.note: When Rav Huna died, the mourners wanted to place a Torah scroll on his bier. Rav Hisda stopped them: Rav Tahlifa had once seen Rav Huna move a Torah scroll off his bed onto an upturned jug before sitting down, so Rav Huna would not have wanted it. The bier would not fit through the door; Rav Hisda refused to let them lower it from the roof or move him to a narrower bier, citing what Rav Huna taught about a scholar's honor, so they broke open the doorway. Rabbi Abba began his eulogy saying Rav Huna was worthy of the Divine Presence but Babylonia prevented it. Rav Nahman bar Hisda objected with a verse about Ezekiel prophesying in Babylonia, and his father tapped him with his sandal to stop him troubling everyone.
moed_katan-25a-8-13.why: The discussion has been about how to honor a dead Torah scholar, as in the Rav Safra case just before. Rav Huna's funeral gives a series of such rules, each taught from Rav Huna's own practice.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A great Sage whose funeral is described.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who directs how Rav Huna's body is to be honored, based on what he learned from him.

people.name: Rav Tahlifa
people.about: Saw Rav Huna move a Torah scroll off his bed before sitting on it.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Gives the opening eulogy for Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Hisda
people.about: Rav Hisda's son, who objects to the eulogy with a verse; some say it was Rav Hanan bar Hisda.

terms.meaning: The frame or stretcher on which a dead body is carried to burial.
The Shekhina, God's presence resting on a person, as in prophecy.
The land of the Jewish community in Mesopotamia (today Iraq), where Rav Huna lived, outside the Land of Israel.

moed_katan-25a-14-20.note: Rav Huna's body was taken to the Land of Israel for burial. Told 'Rav Huna has come,' Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi thought he was alive and said they could barely lift their heads before him in Babylonia; now had he followed them here? Told it was his coffin, they went out to meet it, while Rabbi Hanina (and some say Rabbi Ila) did not. The Sages decided to bury him beside Rabbi Hiyya, and Rav Hagga, who had served Rav Huna and knew his piety, carried him into the cave. There the spirit of Rabbi Hiyya's son Yehuda told his brother Hizkiyya to rise for Rav Huna; when Hizkiyya rose, a pillar of fire rose with him. Rav Hagga, frightened, stood the coffin up and left, and was not harmed.
moed_katan-25a-14-20.why: The Gemara is gathering stories about the deaths and funerals of Sages and how they were honored. It also uses the Sages who did or did not go out to meet the coffin to reconcile two teachings on standing in line for a coffin passing between places.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A great Sage from Babylonia whose body is brought to the Land of Israel for burial.

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sages in the Land of Israel who had once been in awe of Rav Huna in Babylonia; they go out to meet his coffin.

people.name: Rav Hagga
people.about: Rav Huna's former student and attendant, who carries his body into Rabbi Hiyya's burial cave.

people.name: Yehuda and Hizkiyya
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's sons, buried on either side of him; Yehuda tells Hizkiyya to rise for Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who spread Torah in Israel; Rav Huna is buried beside him.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: black leather boxes with Torah verses, strapped to the arm and head during prayer; the straps' black side should face outward.
A blessing said in a line formed to comfort mourners as a funeral passes.
Rav Hagga cites never having had one as a sign of his purity, fitting him to enter the holy burial cave.

moed_katan-25a-23-23.note: When Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna died, both were carried to the Land of Israel. At a bridge, the camels carrying them stopped and would not move. A certain Arab asked why, and was told the dead Sages were showing honor to each other, each telling the other to go first. The Arab said that by law Rabba bar Huna should go first; Rabba bar Huna's camel then crossed, and the Arab's molars and teeth fell out. A child then opened the eulogy, mourning the 'shoot of an ancient line' and the 'book of wars' come up from Babylonia, and saying God rejoices when a righteous soul comes to Him.
moed_katan-25a-23-23.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how great Sages were mourned and brought to burial, following the stories of Rav Huna and Rav Hisda; famous eulogies follow.

people.name: Rabba bar Huna
people.about: A Sage, the son of a great man, whose body is carried to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage great in Torah, carried to burial with Rabba bar Huna.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: A bystander who decides which Sage goes first, and whose teeth fall out.

terms.meaning: A biblical name for Babylonia, where the two Sages had lived.
A phrase from Numbers 21:14 used in the eulogy for Rav Hamnuna, comparing his Torah learning to the book of the Wars of the Lord.

moed_katan-25b-2-2.note: When Ravina died, a certain eulogizer opened his eulogy with the words: 'Date-palms, hang your heads over the righteous man who may be likened to a date-palm. Let us make our nights like days over one who made his nights like days.' The image is of a man who studied Torah through the night, now wept for through the night.
moed_katan-25b-2-2.why: The Gemara is gathering famous eulogies for great Sages, following the eulogy for Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna; the story of two eulogizers who had planned words for Ravina follows.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage whose death is mourned, likened to a date-palm.

people.name: a certain eulogizer
people.about: The unnamed speaker who gives the opening eulogy for Ravina.

terms.meaning: A public speech of mourning praising the dead, often opened with a short poetic verse.

moed_katan-25b-3-5.note: Before Ravina died, Rav Ashi asked the eulogizer bar Kippok what he would say on that day. Bar Kippok answered: 'If the cedars went up in flame, what shall the hyssop of the wall do? If the leviathan was lifted by a hook, what shall the fish of the marsh do?' Another eulogizer, bar Avin, objected that 'hook' and 'flame' must not be said of the righteous, and offered instead: 'Cry for the mourners and not for what was lost; it has gone to rest, and we are left with sighs.' Rav Ashi was offended by them, their feet turned crooked, and on the day Ravina died neither came to eulogize him. Rav Ashi said that neither of them could now perform halitza.
moed_katan-25b-3-5.why: The Gemara is collecting famous eulogies for Sages; this story follows the eulogy actually given for Ravina and tells what happened to the two eulogizers who had prepared their own.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who asks the eulogizers what they will say for Ravina, and is offended by their answers.

people.name: bar Kippok
people.about: A famous eulogizer who compares Ravina to a cedar and others to hyssop.

people.name: bar Avin
people.about: Another eulogizer who objects to bar Kippok's words and offers his own.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage whose coming death the eulogizers are preparing for.

terms.meaning: A ceremony releasing a childless widow from marrying her husband's brother, in which she removes his shoe; crooked feet make it impossible, so Rav Ashi's remark is a pun on their injury.
A small, lowly plant, set against the mighty cedar to contrast the great with the humble.
A giant sea creature of the Bible, here an image of a great man.

moed_katan-25b-8-8.note: Rabbi Hanin was a son-in-law in the house of the Nasi. He had no children, prayed for mercy, and a son was born to him, but on the very day the child was born, Rabbi Hanin died. A eulogizer opened: 'Happiness has been turned into sorrow; joy and suffering have joined together. At the moment of his happiness he sighed; at the moment he was graced, his grace was lost.' They named the child Hanan after him.
moed_katan-25b-8-8.why: This is the first of a run of eulogies for righteous men that the Gemara lists with a memory aid of names, continuing its collection of how great Sages were mourned.

people.name: Rabbi Hanin
people.about: A Sage married into the family of the Nasi, who died on the day his long-prayed-for son was born.

people.name: a certain eulogizer
people.about: The unnamed speaker who opens Rabbi Hanin's eulogy.

terms.meaning: The president or patriarch, the head of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
A play on Rabbi Hanin's name, which sounds like the Hebrew word for grace or favor.

moed_katan-25b-9-9.note: When Rabbi Yohanan died, Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar opened his eulogy: 'Today is as hard for the Jewish people as the day the sun set at noon,' quoting the prophet Amos about the sun going down at noon and feasts turned to mourning. Rabbi Yohanan himself had once taught that this verse refers to the day King Josiah was killed.
moed_katan-25b-9-9.why: The Gemara is working through its list of eulogies for righteous men; after Rabbi Hanin comes Rabbi Yohanan, whose death is likened to the loss of the most righteous person of a generation.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A great Sage whose death is mourned; he had taught that the verse about the sun setting at noon refers to Josiah's death.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar
people.about: Opens the eulogy for Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Josiah
people.about: A biblical king of Judah whose killing Rabbi Yohanan linked to Amos's verse.

terms.meaning: An image from the prophet Amos for sudden darkness in full day, used here for the death of a great leader.

moed_katan-26a-19-20.note: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were sitting before their teacher (the text names him Rabbi Abba as well). He needed to relieve himself, so he took off his head phylacteries and laid them on the cushion, and an ostrich came and tried to swallow them. He said that had it succeeded, he would have been obliged to tear his clothes twice. His companion asked where he got that from: the same thing had happened to him, and when Rav Mattana had no answer, Rav Yehuda told him in Shmuel's name that one tears only when a sacred book is destroyed by force, as in the incident with King Jehoiakim.
moed_katan-26a-19-20.why: Rav Huna had just taught that one who sees a Torah scroll torn must make two tears, for the parchment and the writing, learned from Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll. This story limits that rule to sacred writings destroyed by force.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Removes his phylacteries, nearly loses them to an ostrich, and says he would have had to tear twice.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Sits with Rabbi Abba during the incident.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage who had no answer when asked about a similar case.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who answers the question by quoting Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling is quoted: one tears only when a sacred book is destroyed by force.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the head and arm; they are holy objects, removed before using the toilet.
Two tears in one's clothing, one for the damaged parchment and one for the holy writing on it.

moed_katan-26b-23-23.note: A close relative of Rava died, and Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyomi, came to comfort him. Rava stood the bed upright, as one does for an ordinary visitor, but Abba bar Marta turned it over, treating himself as a close friend. Rava said: 'How lacking in sense is this Torah scholar.'
moed_katan-26b-23-23.why: A teaching just quoted says a visitor sure of his close friendship with the mourner shares the meal of comfort on overturned beds, and otherwise on upright ones. Rava's remark shows a visitor misjudging that line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage in mourning for a close relative.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also known as Abba bar Minyomi; a Torah scholar who visits Rava and overturns the bed.

terms.meaning: A mourning custom: mourners turned their beds over and sat or slept on them during the days of mourning.

moed_katan-27a-2-2.note: When Rabban Gamliel the Elder, the Nasi, died, Rabbi Eliezer told the household to overturn their beds as soon as the body left the doorway of his house. When the tomb was sealed with its cover, Rabbi Yehoshua told them to overturn their beds. They answered him that they had already done so, following the Elder, Rabbi Eliezer.
moed_katan-27a-2-2.why: A teaching just quoted records that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree on when mourners overturn their beds: when the body leaves the house, or when the tomb is sealed. This incident shows each ruling given in practice.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The Nasi, whose death and burial are the setting.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Tells the household to overturn beds once the body leaves the house; called 'the Elder' by them.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells them to overturn beds once the tomb is sealed.

terms.meaning: The president or patriarch, head of the Jewish community and its Sages.
The golel, the stone or slab that seals the tomb.
A mourning custom: the household turns its beds over as a sign of grief.

moed_katan-27b-3-3.note: At first, carrying out the dead for burial was harder on the relatives than the death itself, because of the cost of the burial clothes, until relatives would leave the body and run away. Then Rabban Gamliel set his own dignity aside and was carried out for burial in linen garments, and the people followed his practice. Rav Pappa adds that nowadays everyone is buried even in plain hemp garments costing a dinar.
moed_katan-27b-3-3.why: The Gemara is listing changes the Sages made to funeral practice out of respect for the poor and the embarrassed, such as plain biers and incense for all. Rabban Gamliel's simple burial is one more change of this kind.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A leader who chose to be buried in simple linen, and the people followed him.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who says that in his day even cheap hemp garments are used.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of small value; here a sign of how cheap the burial garments had become.

moed_katan-27b-12-12.note: Rav Hamnuna came to a place called Darumata and heard the shofar announcing that someone in the town had died. Seeing people at work, he said: 'Let these people be under excommunication. Is there not a dead person in town?' They told him the town had separate groups, each caring for its own dead. He said: 'If so, it is permitted to you.'
moed_katan-27b-12-12.why: Rav had just ruled that when someone dies in a city, all its residents may not work until the burial. Rav Hamnuna's visit shows the rule in action, and limits it where a town is divided into groups that each tend their own dead.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage visiting Darumata who places the townspeople working during a death under excommunication, then permits them.

terms.meaning: A ram's horn; here blown to announce a death in the town.
A ban placing a person outside the community's normal dealings, a penalty the Sages could impose.

moed_katan-27b-13-13.note: A woman in Rav Huna's neighborhood had seven sons. One died and she wept for him excessively. Rav Huna sent word: 'Do not do this,' but she took no heed. He sent again: 'If you listen to me, well; if not, prepare shrouds for another death.' She did not listen, and all of them died. At last he told her to prepare shrouds for herself, and she died.
moed_katan-27b-13-13.why: Rav had just taught that anyone who grieves excessively over his dead will end up weeping for another. The story illustrates that warning, and the Gemara goes on to set the proper limits of mourning.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who warns a grieving neighbor to stop her excessive weeping.

people.name: a certain woman
people.about: Rav Huna's neighbor, a mother of seven sons who mourns one of them excessively.

terms.meaning: The cloth garments in which the dead are wrapped for burial.

moed_katan-28a-10-10.note: When Rav Yosef turned sixty, he made a holiday for the Sages, saying: 'I have passed the age of karet.' Abaye said to him: 'Even if you have escaped the karet of years, have you escaped the karet of days?' Rav Yosef answered: 'Grasp at least half in your hand.'
moed_katan-28a-10-10.why: The Gemara has been reading the age at which a person dies as a sign: death at fifty to sixty is death by karet, and sudden death is another kind. Rav Yosef's celebration at sixty, and Abaye's reply, apply both readings.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who celebrates his sixtieth birthday with a feast for the Sages.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who reminds Rav Yosef that he could still suffer sudden death.

terms.meaning: Literally 'cutting off': a divine punishment for the gravest sins, here taken to show itself as death before sixty or a sudden death.

moed_katan-28a-16-16.note: Rav Seorim, Rava's brother, sat before Rava and saw that he was dozing, that is, about to die. Rava asked him to tell the Angel of Death not to torment him. Rav Seorim asked: 'Are you not his friend?' Rava answered that once his fate was handed over, the Angel paid him no heed. Rav Seorim asked him to appear to him after his death, and Rava did. Asked whether dying had hurt, Rava said: 'Like the prick of the knife when letting blood.'
moed_katan-28a-16-16.why: The Gemara has been discussing what the timing of death means and has turned to the deaths of the righteous; this is the first of several accounts of Sages describing their own deaths.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage on his deathbed who later appears to his brother in a dream.

people.name: Rav Seorim
people.about: Rava's brother, who sits with him as he dies.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: The angel who takes life; Rava asks that he not torment him.

terms.meaning: Bloodletting, a common medical treatment in which a small cut is made to release blood; the prick of the knife was a slight pain.

moed_katan-28a-17-18.note: Rava was sitting with Rav Nahman as Rav Nahman was slipping into death. Rav Nahman asked Rava to tell the Angel of Death not to torment him. Rava answered that surely Rav Nahman was an important man in Heaven's eyes, but Rav Nahman replied that in the world above no one counts as important, honorable or complete. Rava asked him to appear in a dream after his death, and he did: dying, he said, was as painless as pulling a hair out of milk, yet if God told him to go back to life as before he would refuse, because the fear of the Angel of Death is so great.
moed_katan-28a-17-18.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous died. This one comes right after the near-identical exchange between Rava and his brother Rav Seorim, and pairs with it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who sits with Rav Nahman at his death and later asks him in a dream what dying was like.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage on his deathbed who asks Rava to plead with the Angel of Death for him.

people.name: the Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, whom Rav Nahman imagines offering to send him back to life.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28a-19-19.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rabbi Elazar while he was eating teruma. Rabbi Elazar objected that teruma is called sacred, so it would be wrong to die in the middle of eating it. The moment passed and he was spared.
moed_katan-28a-19-19.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death. This is the first of a run of stories in which a Sage talks back to the Angel of Death.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who argues the Angel of Death out of taking him while he eats teruma.

terms.meaning: The portion of the harvest given to the priests. It is holy food, eaten only by priests and their households in a state of ritual purity.
In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28a-20-20.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rav Sheshet in the marketplace. Rav Sheshet protested: should he die in the street like an animal? He told the Angel of Death to come to his house instead.
moed_katan-28a-20-20.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death. This follows the story of Rabbi Elazar, another Sage who tells the Angel of Death when and where he may take him.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who refuses to die in the marketplace and sends the Angel of Death to his home.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28a-21-21.note: The Angel of Death appeared to Rav Ashi in the marketplace. Rav Ashi asked for thirty days to review his learning, since in Heaven they say that happy is the one who arrives with his learning in hand. On the thirtieth day the Angel of Death came back. When Rav Ashi asked why he was in such a hurry, the angel answered that Rav Huna bar Natan, his successor, was already pressing at his heels, and one reign may not overlap another by even a hair's breadth.
moed_katan-28a-21-21.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous faced death; this follows the stories of Rabbi Elazar and Rav Sheshet, who also bargain with the Angel of Death.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who wins thirty days from the Angel of Death to review his studies.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Natan
people.about: Named by the Angel of Death as the man ready to succeed Rav Ashi as leader.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28a-22-22.note: The Angel of Death could not take Rav Hisda, because his mouth never stopped reciting his studies. So the angel went and sat on the cedar beam of the study hall. The cedar cracked, Rav Hisda fell silent for a moment, and in that moment the angel was able to take him.
moed_katan-28a-22-22.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how the righteous died; this follows a run of Sages who hold off the Angel of Death, here by unbroken Torah study.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage whose constant study keeps the Angel of Death away from him.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28a-23-23.note: The Angel of Death could not get near Rabbi Hiyya. One day he disguised himself as a poor man, knocked at the door and asked for bread, and Rabbi Hiyya brought it out to him. Then the angel said: you have mercy on a poor man, so why have you no mercy on me? He revealed who he was and showed Rabbi Hiyya a rod of fire, and Rabbi Hiyya gave himself up to him.
moed_katan-28a-23-23.why: This is the last in the Gemara's series about how the righteous died, many of them resisting the Angel of Death; after it the Gemara turns to the next mishna, on mourning during the Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage the Angel of Death cannot approach until he tricks him with a request for charity.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic stories, the angel sent by God to take a person's life at the appointed time.

moed_katan-28b-10-18.note: When Rabbi Yishmael's sons died, four elders came to comfort him: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Tarfon warned the others not to interrupt one another, and Rabbi Akiva asked to speak last. Rabbi Yishmael opened by blaming his own many sins for his repeated losses. Each elder then quoted a verse about a biblical figure who did only one good deed yet was mourned or honored at death (the sons of Aaron, Abijah son of Jeroboam, King Zedekiah, King Ahab) and argued that the sons of Rabbi Yishmael deserve all the more. Along the way the Gemara pauses to ask what Abijah's good deed was, and Rav Yosef says he would not understand Rabbi Akiva's verse without its Aramaic translation.
moed_katan-28b-10-18.why: The Gemara has been gathering teachings on mourning and eulogies, such as Rabbi Meir's saying that whoever eulogizes others will be eulogized; this baraita shows Sages comforting a mourner. Afterward Rava questions how the verses about Zedekiah and Josiah fit together.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A great Sage, learned in aggada, whose sons have died.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: One of the four elders who comes to comfort Rabbi Yishmael; he sets the rule that no one interrupt.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: One of the four comforters; he speaks of Abijah son of Jeroboam.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: One of the four comforters; he speaks of King Zedekiah.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of the four comforters, who asks to speak last; he speaks of the mourning in Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.
An argument from the lesser to the greater: if something is true in a weaker case, it is all the more true in a stronger one.
The non-legal teachings of the Sages: stories, sayings and interpretations of Scripture.
The Targum, an ancient Aramaic rendering of the Bible, which here explains an obscure verse.
